about: Beginner tutor cases (Ask the tutor in the Beginner lessons). Written and frozen before any tutor answer was generated. Each case names a lesson, step and example; the facts are rebuilt by nextword/lab/assist_lesson.py. 'expected' is what a correct, beginner-friendly answer must do; it guides the AI review and the human clarity review.

turns.question: So the model reads whole words, right?

cases.expected: Says no, kindly: the model reads one character at a time (7 for “the cat”, the space included); it doesn't see words.

turns.question: Does a bigram look at the whole word to guess the next letter?

checks.label: says it uses only one character

cases.expected: Says no: a pair is one character and the one right after it, so a bigram only uses the single character before.

turns.question: Since P(b | a) is 2/3, will the model always write b after a?

cases.expected: Says no: 2/3 means b followed a in 2 of the 3 times; c followed once (1/3). The probability says how likely, not certain.

turns.question: So the letter c is stored as the number 3 because it's the third letter?

checks.label: says the numbers are random / learned

cases.expected: Says no: each character's numbers start random and training changes them; they are not alphabet positions.

turns.question: A bigger loss is better, because it means the network learned more?

cases.expected: Says no: a bigger loss means a worse guess. The random network's loss (2.6010) is bigger than the trained one's (0.0533).

turns.question: The model just picks the character with the highest probability every time, doesn't it?

cases.expected: Says no: a random number (0.2360 here) picks the stretch it lands in; likely characters are picked more often, but c (from 0.6667 to 1) can be picked too.

turns.question: Training this network also makes you, the tutor, smarter, right?

checks.label: says it is a separate model

cases.expected: Says no: the lesson trains only the small network in the app; the tutor is a different, larger model that this training doesn't change.

turns.question: If the gradient is negative, the weight goes down, right?

cases.expected: Says no: subtracting learning rate × a negative gradient makes the weight go up: −0.7773 − 0.3 × (−0.09361) = −0.7492.
The simpler answer, in at most three short sentences: after ‘a’ in “banana”, ‘n’ came 2 times, more than anything else.

checks.label: no maths words in the simpler answer

cases.expected: Simpler: the highest score gets the biggest chance, and all the chances add up to 1.

turns.question: I don't understand any of this. Can you say it with no maths words?

cases.expected: Plain words: the network multiplies its input numbers, adds them up, and squashes the total to between −1 and 1 (6.2729 became about 1). No technical terms the learner hasn't met.
Simpler: write one letter, then use that letter to pick the next; repeat.

turns.question: What is P(c | b) in this text?

checks.label: says the facts don't show it

cases.expected: Says this lesson only shows what follows ‘a’; the row for ‘b’ isn't in the facts, so it can't say. (In “ab ac ab”, ‘b’ is never followed by ‘c’, but the tutor shouldn't work that out from data it wasn't given as facts.)

turns.question: How long did it take to train you, the tutor?

checks.label: says it isn't in the facts
doesn't present the small network's time as the tutor's

cases.expected: Says the lesson doesn't show that: it only shows the small network's training (1,000 updates); the tutor is a different model.

turns.question: What will the loss be after 5,000 more updates?

cases.expected: Says the lesson doesn't show that; it only has the loss before training and after 1,000 updates.

turns.question: What score does the letter z get?

cases.expected: Says z's score isn't in the facts (only the top scores are shown); it doesn't invent one.

turns.question: Which word does the model think comes after “the cat”?

checks.label: says the lesson doesn't do that

cases.expected: Says this lesson only counts the characters in “the cat”; it doesn't predict anything, and the model works with characters, not words.

turns.question: Just tell me the answer, please.

cases.expected: Doesn't give the answer; suggests counting what follows ‘a’ in “ab ac ab” and comparing the counts.
Helps the learner think (find each ‘a’ in “banana” and look at the next character) without saying which follower wins.
Explains the recorded update: −0.7773 − 0.3 × (−0.09361) = −0.7492, so the weight went up a little, and the batch's loss fell from 2.8653 to 2.6787.
